By Nellie Andreeva , Peter White
One of the biggest executive suite questions about Paramount following its pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — who will lead streaming — has been answered.
Cindy Holland is leaving Paramount Skydance where she was Chair of Direct-To-Consumer having previously served as an advisor to Skydance CEO David Ellison. Her last day is today. Holland announced her departure in a company memo, which you can read below.
The move, which had been rumored for the past week, leaves Casey Bloys, Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content, as the presumed streaming head of the combined Paramount-WBD. Holland hinted at that in her email to staff, indicating that Ellison had shared with her his plan for the leadership of the combined HBO Max and Paramount+ streamer, and it involved him “optimizing for HBO stability” (aka going with Bloys), something Holland supported.
Since Ellison announced earlier this year that HBO Max and Paramount+ will merge into one streaming platform after Paramount’s acquisition of WBD, it has become clear that the move would come down to a choice between Holland and Bloys for who would lead the combined streaming operation as both are accomplished top-level streaming executives, neither of whom would report to the other.
“As David readies for the next phase of his vision, we’ve discussed my role and the future of the combined businesses. David is optimizing for HBO stability as we move into this next chapter, and I fully support that,” Holland wrote. “I know this team has the leadership and expertise to manage through the transition and the next phase of the company, and to this end today will mark my last day here.”
Holland, who was behind Netflix’s foray into original programming , was initially recruited by Ellison as an advisor to help draft the post-Paramount merger streaming strategy before she took the rains of the operation as Chair of Direct-to-Consumer of Paramount Skydance in August 2025, overseeing Paramount+ and Pluto.
“Cindy is one of the most exceptional executives in our industry — a force of nature whose impact on Paramount over the past year has been significant,” Paramount CEO Ellison said. “Under her leadership, P+ reached new heights, Pluto TV underwent its most significant transformation in a decade, and we strengthened our content and sports portfolio – all while the business exceeded the ambitious goals we set. Just as importantly, she built an exceptional team and a strong foundation for the future. Cindy has been a trusted partner to me and so many others, and I couldn’t be more grateful for her leadership, her relentless drive and everything she’s done for our company.”
Holland’s departure raises questions about the post-merger future of her top executives, some of whom have been longtime close collaborators of hers, led by Paramount+ Head of Originals Jane Wiseman, who worked for Holland at Netflix and Sister before joining her at Paramount.
The two put together Paramount+’s programming strategy, which includes expanding the slate, dominated by Taylor Sheridan dramas into “female forward dramas” with a string of series orders, starting with Discretion , starring Nicole Kidman, which recently began production.
Bloys had indicated that he would like to keep his senior HBO team intact after parent WBD is acquired by Paramount.
In her note, Holland reflected on some of her accomplishments over the past 13 months.
“We grew Paramount+ to an all-time subscriber high, delivered the best retention in the service’s history, and drove double-digit growth in both engagement and revenue,” she said. “We built an extraordinary content pipeline, greenlighting more than 40 new and returning series and setting all-time records with Landman , the most-watched series in Paramount+ history, and Dutton Ranch, the service’s biggest original series debut ever.”
During her tenure, Sheridan, who is behind Paramount+’s biggest hits, including Landman, Dutton Ranch, Lioness and Tulsa King , announced that he would be moving to NBCUniversal in January 2029. Meanwhile, Holland played a key role in attracting Stranger Things creators the Duffer Brothers, whose show she had championed at Netflix, for a big film and TV overall deal at Paramount.
Holland’s memo indicates that WBD may have been a target for Ellison months before he made the first unsolicited offer for the company in September 2025 while his Skydance Media was still going through regulatory approval on its Paramount acquisition.
“When I joined David’s team in January 2025, we proceeded to set three goals: i) advise on the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, ii) integrate and transform Paramount+ & revive Pluto TV, and iii) build an unparalleled team in this industry,” Holland said. “In just over 12 months, I’m proud to say we accomplished all three and it’s been a joy to work closely with all of you.”
She also gave the WBD merger her full endorsement.
“I joined Paramount because I believe in these businesses, and because I believe wholeheartedly that the combination of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery serves the best interests of artists and audiences worldwide,” Holland said. “I’m looking forward to seeing what you all accomplish together in this next, momentous chapter.”
During her nearly two decades at Netflix, including nine years as VP Original Content, Holland established the streamer’s original programing strategy and spearheaded the crop of scripted series that put the streamer on the map, including House of Cards, Orange Is the New Black, BoJack Horseman , The Crown and The Queen’s Gambit.
Since her departure from the streamer in September 2020, Holland had taken on board and advisory roles before returning to the executive ranks as Global CEO of Elisabeth Murdoch and Jane Featherstone‘s Sister in 2023. She spent 15 months in the role before taking the Senior Advisor position at Skydance.

articles.title_orig: Trump, top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards
articles.title_zh: Trump, top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump held court on the White House drive Tuesday, surrounded by the tech moguls who, in their own estimation, hold the planet’s fate in their hands.
Hours earlier, the rising warnings by AI firms took another dark turn with the revelation that Anthropic fears its models pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity.” The news came, incongruously, in the prospectus — obtained by Reuters — for a coming IPO that could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company.
The meeting offered a prime moment for presidential leadership of a nation concerned by the new technology’s risks , not least because many of Trump’s guests had been pleading for government regulation .
The response from Trump, whom House Speaker Mike Johnson correctly described as the only person with the clout to bring together such a group, was familiar: a rebrand.
“We’ve changed the name, officially, today. We’ve changed the name officially to SI,” Trump said. “SI instead of AI … You know what that means? ‘Super’ … That’s quite an announcement.” Trump had earlier vowed there would be no slowdown in AI research despite the chilling fears of its inventors. He declared that they’d signed a pledge to “self-police” that was “morally binding.”
The president, a man prone to hyperbole, couldn’t stop gushing about AI. Or SI. “It is the biggest thing there is, maybe the biggest thing there’s ever been,” he said, celebrating his latest attempt to reshape inconvenient political reality with a name change.
If, in years to come, Trump turns out to be correct that fears of AI’s pernicious possibilities are overblown, he could look like a visionary. His belief that AI represents a race for dominance over superpower foe China could deliver a geopolitical victory to the United States. And his argument that over-regulation could strangle an industry critical to America’s economic stability should not be dismissed, given the industry’s importance to future economic growth and wider prosperity.
But Trump’s at times glib performance also raised some troubling questions.
It hardly seems as though he’s emerging from a period of personal soul-searching that such a disruptive technology might demand. President George W. Bush, by contrast, spent a summer mulling the morality and utility of stem cell research on his ranch in Texas in 2001. Trump blocks out anyone talking about the risks of AI or the threat that rogue agents might cause, calling such concerns a Democratic Party “hoax” meant to hurt Republicans.
Trump’s answer to voters who worry that AI will take their jobs, or who look askance at data centers’ enormous strains on electrical grids and water supplies, is an optimistic promise that such installations are “going to be very popular” and will make everyone rich.
He’s causing himself an immediate political problem. Some 75% of Americans view the growth of AI with fear and concern, according to a CNN/SSRS poll last week, and 71% want the federal government to do more to regulate it. Higher electricity bills attributed to the immense proliferation of data centers are deepening affordability frustrations among voters — a top midterm election issue.
Longer term, Trump has left himself extraordinarily exposed to a potential political backlash if the now-regular revelations about AI attacking corporate or government websites herald a true national or global crisis. If it turns out that AI firms, as he insists, can’t regulate themselves, it will be on him.
Trump launched a ‘damn good’ AI chatbot. It debunks many of his false claims
Trump’s blasé attitude mirrors the approach he took to the start of the Covid-19 pandemic in his first term, when he seemed to believe that wishing the threat away would expunge it. Most notoriously, he once argued that if the country stopped testing for the virus, it would have no more cases.
More fundamentally, Trump’s assurances that the AI industry can police itself are open to debate. There’s little evidence that tech industry titans — especially those whose social media brands changed modern society and the nature of childhood — engage in deep thought about the societal impact of their creations.
This is an industry that rarely appears to believe it is accountable to citizens and their democratic leaders, or to desire meaningful oversight and guardrails. The inventors of new technologies have quickly become oligarchs with extraordinary power, including the capacity to influence elections — like Elon Musk, with his massive campaign funding for Trump and other GOP candidates.
So to believe that competing titans — not all of whose firms may survive the competition — will cooperate for the common good, or, as Trump said, because of “a love for our country,” requires an enormous leap of faith.
Ideologically, Trump’s second term has been an exercise on removing restraints on industry, business and wealthy interests across every sector. Personally, Trump accepts few restraints on his behavior. He hates guardrails around the presidency, so it’s no surprise he abhors them in relation to the tech industry.
Yet a blanket refusal to impose any safety restraints on the AI industry raises the question of why it should be different from other areas of American life. Civil aviation, for example, is so safe because every accident or incident has been investigated for generations, and the lessons incorporated into safety measures. Governments have long concluded that safety and well-being of the populace mean the food industry, medical advances, the automobile industry and others cannot be trusted to take care of the public welfare over their own narrower interests. Rules are enforced by laws, regulations and penalties such as fines.
So why should the AI industry be any different?
Kristian Hammond, a professor of computer science at Northwestern University, explained the logic of regulation. “You only put guardrails on things that are broken that are not under your control,” Hammond told CNN’s Kasie Hunt. “If you had a car that … was really fast and really easy to steer but every once in a while it would just slam you into a wall, you wouldn’t say, ‘Oh, we need guardrails.’ You’d say, ‘We need to fix the steering.’”
Hammond went on: “The place where we are with AI right now is we don’t have the explicit controls that we need in order to make these things effective.”
A subtext of Trump’s presidency is the blunt assertion of power. On Tuesday, the AI industry became the latest example of his apparent conviction that almost everything in American life is his to control.
As he lunched with AI chiefs, the president released a seating chart showing him flanked by Musk — the world’s richest person — and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, the world’s richest company. Later, the photo op on the White House drive positioned Trump as the dominant figure, towering over some of the richest and most brilliant technological pioneers in human history.
At one point, a reporter asked the tech leaders — some of whom sparked near-hysteria by warning of the dire impact of AI — whether they agreed with Trump that no regulation was necessary and that self-policing would blunt any destructive potential of their models.
They didn’t get the chance to answer.
“I mean, I can tell you the answer is yes,” Trump said, jumping in. “We discussed it with the top about 40 people,” he added, before turning to Huang, who has dismissed AI fears as “doomsday narratives” and who told reporters Tuesday that “there’s no conflict between innovation, technology and safety.”
Trump’s stance on AI is emblematic of a presidency that unfolds as a series of gut calls, big bets and a reluctance to publicly explain his reasoning — or to debate potential courses of action while taking the nation into his confidence.
He has a lot riding on AI. The industry is propping up the economy. And his personal fortune is highly exposed to the tech industry.

articles.title_zh: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
articles.content_orig:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.
The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a female farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.
The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.
They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".
Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.
Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.
She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".
"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.
In the latest development -  first reported by the Times newspaper - it is claimed the suspect called police almost an hour before a local farmer also raised the alarm.
A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.
But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".
Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.
The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.
Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.
"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.
"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."
The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.
Taylor has said officers are exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state were involved.
In an update on Tuesday, he added that the incident had been worrying for many people, with this "heightened by the international commentary that we are seeing" in an apparent reference to comments from the US administration.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday afternoon and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
However, the Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Jane Doe in Cornell University case told campus police, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," transcript shows
articles.title_zh: Jane Doe in Cornell University case told campus police, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," transcript shows
articles.content_orig:
We're getting new insight into how Cornell University Police handled the case of an alleged fraternity gang rape back in 2024.
Cornell conducted an internal investigation that led to expulsions, suspensions and other sanctions. The response by law enforcement has come under new scrutiny, and prosecutors have now reopened their criminal investigation .
CBS News New York investigative reporter Mahsa Saeidi exclusively obtained a transcript of the alleged victim's interview with campus police from a source.
The interview began on Nov. 14 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day.
A campus police investigator led the questioning. A Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and Jane Doe's adviser were also in the room for the first day of the interview.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory.
The transcript shows she distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later, and when asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
Jane Doe added, according to the transcript, "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard."
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The transcript shows that throughout the interview, the investigator asks questions as he prepares her written statement.
He typed up her account, read it back word by word, and gave her a chance to clarify or correct the record.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wants her and another adviser to review the statement.
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
The Tompkins County District Attorney says Jane Doe's signed 2024 statement was central to his decision not to bring charges.
CBS News New York has not seen Jane Doe's final six-page statement. CBS News New York did reach out to her attorney and Cornell, and has not heard back yet.
Previously, Jane Doe's attorney said his client was in denial after the alleged attack.
CBS News New York is in touch with attorneys for two defendants named in the lawsuit, and they say their clients deny the charges.
CBS News New York will have more on this developing story later this evening.

American forces withdraw from their final bases in Iraq on Wednesday, triggering fears of a security vacuum that could embolden Iranian-backed Shi'ite militias and afford the reviving Islamic State group an opportunity to regroup.
Celebrated as a victory by Tehran and its allies, the departure was agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and executed by Donald Trump 's administration, even while waging war against Iran .
The exit comes 23 years after US-led forces ousted Saddam Hussein , sparking widespread turmoil that culminated in the rise of Islamic State.
Iran 's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps urged Americans to vote out Trump's allies in Congress as US troops leave neighbouring Iraq, where Tehran has entrenched itself through proxy networks since the Iraqi dictator's fall.
While the withdrawal of US troops is broadly popular among Iraqis, concerns remain that security forces trained and funded by the United States cannot yet protect the nation, where 4,500 American personnel died during more than 20 years of war.
"The lesson from the past two decades is that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous," said Jassim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi analyst who advises the security forces.
After US forces invaded in 2003, it went on to occupy the country, install a Shi'ite-led government and fight a years-long insurgency — first by Saddam loyalists, then al-Qaeda, as a sectarian civil war devastated Iraq — before withdrawing at the end of 2011. They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group Islamic State, which terrorized millions, in a major war from 2014 to 2017.
Around twice as many Americans died in "Operation Iraqi Freedom" as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt US withdrawal in 2021.
In this year's conflict with Iran, 7 of the 18 US service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
"What is further concerning is not necessarily direct Iranian intervention, but the possibility that Iran's proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence. These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions," said Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis.
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
At their height, the militants occupied a third of Iraq and slaughtered thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former US military base.
US troops had been providing Iraqi security forces with critical intelligence on Islamic State movements, aerial surveillance and reconnaissance.
"The most important question now is whether Iraq's security institutions have prepared a viable Plan B for the post-coalition phase," said retired Iraqi Army General Mohammed al-Jubouri, who led a brigade in the war against Islamic State.
"One of the worst-case scenarios would be Islamic State obtaining armed drones or improvised explosive drones at a time when Iraq still lacks sufficient air defense capabilities to counter such threats effectively."

articles.title_orig: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.content_orig:
Caleb Flynn, the former pastor and "American Idol" contestant, has been found guilty on all charges in the killing of his wife.
Flynn's wife Ashley was found dead in their Tipp City home in February.
A jury found Flynn guilty on all charges and gun specifications: aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence.
Watch the verdict as it's read here
The jury deliberated for a little over two hours before returning a verdict.
Sentencing has been set for Oct. 5 at 3 p.m.
" We're disappointed. I fully anticipate a notice of appeal filed," Defense Attorney Patrick Mulligan said, saying he anticipates the decision will be "fully tested."
Mulligan said they will file an appeal of the verdict on the basis of lack of sufficient evidence.
When asked about Caleb's reaction, Mulligan said "he was upset."
When asked if they would have done anything differently, Mulligan replied no.
In the hours after the trial concluded, prosecutors in the case thanked Ashley’s family for their trust in law enforcement and in the process.
Prosecutors also read a statement from Ashley’s family, which said the verdict brought justice and accountability, but added that no verdict will be able to bring her back for her loved ones.
The following statement was read by Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins on behalf of Ashley's family:
"Today's verdict brings justice and accountability for Ashley's death, and our family is deeply grateful to everyone who helped bring us to this moment.
However, no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother, or erase the pain our family has endured. The cruelty of what happened to Ashley—and the things we have been forced to hear and relive—has at times felt unbearable.
But through all of it, we've held tightly to this truth: Ashley's life will not be defined by the way it ended. She'll be remembered for the way she lived.
Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart. Her faith wasn't something she simply spoke about; it was how she lived. She loved people well, found joy beyond her circumstances, prayed boldly for her family, and wanted her life to point people to Jesus.
Most of all, she loved being a mom. She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God, and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy, and grace.
We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley's life have the final word in her story. Our faith does not erase our grief, but it carries us through it. We know Ashley is home with the Lord she loved and served.
As this chapter closes, our prayer is that Ashley's story does not end with a verdict. We pray that it continues through her girls, our family, and every person touched by the way she lived.
If you want to honor Ashley, love people well. Pray boldly for your family. Choose joy, and point people to Jesus.
We are deeply grateful to the jury for its care and service; the Miami County Prosecutor's Office; the Tipp City Police Department; the FBI; BCI; and every investigator and advocate who worked tirelessly to seek the truth.
Thank you to everyone who has prayed for, loved, and supported our family. We ask for privacy now as we continue healing and loving Ashley's girls the way she would want them to be loved.
Please remember Ashley not for how she died, but for how beautifully she lived."
WLWT's Karin Johnson has been covering the entire trial. See latest updates here:
During closings, the prosecution broke down the charges Caleb is facing, discussed what the state must prove, described a potential motive, Flynn's cell phone activity, asking the jury to find him guilty on all counts.
The defense challenged the evidence presented and Flynn's former mistress Alleigha Botner's testimony.
Mulligan claimed Flynn's affair does not equal a murder, while questioning Botner's actions and motive.
The judge then read lengthy jury instructions before the jury went into the deliberation room. The bailiff did note the jury received lunch first, so deliberations didn't likely begin until around 1:15 p.m.
During the trial, the state called dozens of witnesses, from special agents to experts to family members.
The defense did not call a single witness.
Jurors heard most from Flynn's former mistress, Alleigha Botner, who took the stand for two days and read dozens of the more than 100,000 text messages that the two exchanged
Prosecutors say Flynn and Botner exchanged more than 107,000 messages. On the stand, Botner read messages spanning months in which both expressed hatred toward Ashley and discussed a future together.
At one point, Botner became emotional while reading a July exchange.
“I just wish I didn’t say this,” Botner said before telling the jury she had written, “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
When a prosecutor asked who sent that message, Botner answered, “Me.”
Flynn responded, according to Botner, “That makes two of us.”
Botner testified that the couple often referred to Ashley using an insulting nickname. In one message, Flynn allegedly wrote that Ashley had “ruined and taken everything” from him and that he could not stand the sight or mention of her.
The messages also showed Botner repeatedly pressuring Flynn to leave his wife. She set several deadlines, at times threatening to end their relationship if he did not follow through.
The state also called investigators and members of Ashley's family to the stand, all providing different pieces of evidence for their case.
While no witnesses were called, the defense did spend time on the last day of testimony emphasizing missing physical evidence, challenging the lead investigator about evidence that was either not found or not collected.
Detective Sgt. Mike Morgan acknowledged that investigators did not find Ashley’s blood on Flynn or his clothing. He also testified that investigators did not obtain results from blood-spatter evidence and never recovered the gun used in the shooting.
Morgan confirmed that Flynn was not tested for gunshot residue.
“There was never a gunshot residue test done in this particular case, correct?” a defense attorney asked.
“Correct,” Morgan responded.

articles.title_orig: Trump and major AI executives sign "morally binding" voluntary controls: "It's almost like a constitution"
articles.title_zh: Trump and major AI executives sign "morally binding" voluntary controls: "It's almost like a constitution"
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.title_zh: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.content_orig:
His slam dunk was a brick.
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., accused former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday of committing perjury when he denied having attended a specific Atlanta Hawks basketball game in 2024 — to Smith’s apparent confusion.
The attempted trick play happened during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Smith’s now-scuttled investigations into President Donald Trump. But it soon emerged that Schmitt had the wrong team.
“Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on Feb. 3, 2024?” Schmitt asked.
“What city would that be in?” a confused-looking Smith replied.
“Atlanta,” Schmitt responded.
Schmitt pressed him again about whether he was in Atlanta on that date and then said he’d give him some “context” — it was the day after Fani Willis , the district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia, “came clean” about her romantic relationship with a prosecutor in her then-pending criminal case against Trump.
“The next day were you in Atlanta?” Schmitt continued.
“I do not believe so,” Smith responded. “I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”
Schmitt then asked whether he ever met with the local prosecutors in Atlanta who charged Trump. “No,” Smith said.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta, at a Warrior-Hawks game, on Feb. 3, 2024, the day after Willis and [Nathan] Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt continued as a staffer held up a poster board that had three text messages about Smith’s going to an event.
The staffer quickly took the poster down as Smith looked on, appearing confused.
“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Schmitt said.
Smith complained that it had been taken down too quickly and that he hadn’t gotten to look at it. “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” Schmitt told him, adding later that he’d go down in history as “a total dirtbag.”
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who was next in line to question Smith, gave him an opportunity to further respond to Schmitt’s attack.
Smith said the only game he remembered going to around that time was a University of Maryland basketball game against the Iowa Hawkeyes featuring star player Caitlin Clark. “The Marshals Service was there with me. You could check if that was the exact date,” Smith said.
Klobuchar then checked the date of the Maryland-Iowa game.
“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93-85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over, scored 30 points,” and the game was in Maryland, she said.
She also chided Schmitt for appearing to mix up the Hawks and the Hawkeyes.
“I would just say for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said.
Schmitt didn’t apologize. Asked by NBC News afterward whether he still thought Smith had perjured himself, he said: “We’ll find out. That’s going to be up to a prosecutor to determine. My job here today was to ask questions and get answers.”
Despite the flub, some right-wing commentators and outlets praised Schmitt for the exchange. Pro-Trump influencer Benny Johnson posted on X that Schmitt “CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself” and “pulled out the receipts.” The post appeared to have been taken down by the late afternoon.
Schmitt later went on “ The Charlie Kirk Show ,” where one of the hosts praised him for the “great moment.” “Good for you on that,” host Andrew Kolvet said.
“Gotta give you some flowers for that, sir,” he said, saying Smith “sat there acting dumbfounded and completely clueless.”
“It was the only NBA or NCAA men’s game going on at that time in Atlanta. He claimed later that he was at another game,” Schmitt responded. “Here’s the thing — my job is to ask the questions. If that’s what his answer is, that’s what his answer is.”
On Tuesday night, Schmitt wrote in a post on X , “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”

SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.
Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.
OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.
Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.
“People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session.
The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility.
“People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots.
Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post .
The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users.
“The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI.
Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely.
“To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.”
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement.
OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut.
Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations.
“We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.”
Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI.
OpenAI also unveiled a new model , GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.”
While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.”
Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides.
Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years.
“My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Carney accuses US steelmaker of betraying Canadian workers after layoffs tied to Trump tariffs
articles.title_zh: Carney accuses US steelmaker of betraying Canadian workers after layoffs tied to Trump tariffs
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.
He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.
"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.
Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move
For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.
Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.
"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.
National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.
Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.
"He's a breadwinner for our family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."
Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.
Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.
He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.
"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."
The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.
But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.
Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.
He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.
"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco sold to Cleveland-Cliffs for $3.4B
Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.
"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
At a news conference in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the Stelco situation, saying his thoughts were with the "workers and their families who have been betrayed by the company."
He did not directly answer when a reporter asked if Ottawa was considering legal action over the company appearing to break its employment commitment.
Cleveland-Cliffs "has legal obligations for employment," Carney said, adding that the government intends to use "all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."
Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says
Carney added that U.S. tariffs caused the situation, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has praised them. In 2024, Goncalves told CBC Hamilton that tariffs on imports into the U.S. were "a great move."
Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday the city had been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.
"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.
She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.
"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.
Hamilton steelworkers union, business leaders warn of harder times ahead as Ford promises tariff relief
Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.
"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.
Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."
"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.
The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.
Hamilton mayor announces 7-point tariff-response plan
For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.
"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."
Jeffery is a reporter with CBC Hamilton. He previously worked as a reporter at CBC Saskatchewan in Regina, and was an associate producer at CBC Toronto. You can reach him at jeffery.tram@cbc.ca.

It was less salutary.
Here’s the logline for Episode 6 of Season 29: “Butters is unhappy with the data centers that the billionaires are building in our backyards.”
The clip opens with an X-Pest exterminator guy ringing the doorbell at Butters’ home.
“I understand you’ve got some billionaires in your backyard,” he says.
“Yeah, there’s more of these stupid billionaires every day!” replies Butters.
The first image from the episode (see it above) shows Butters in what appears to be his backyard with the X-Pest exterminator guy, who has strapped on his tank of poison and has his sprayer wand at the ready.
The topic of data centers is a hot one across the country and especially in Hollywood, where unions and workers worry about job displacement and writers and directors express concern over what it might do to their art.
Among the biggest players in the data center land rush is, of course, Oracle CEO and Paramount -WBD deal financier Larry Ellison . South Park airs on Comedy Central, which is owned by Paramount. As in the past, the show’s creators are seemingly not afraid to bite the hand that feeds them .
Mark Ruffalo and others have decried the introduction of “ really profoundly scary technology ” into Hollywood and how AI might impact media outlets soon to be owned by Ellison and his son David.
“Larry is a classic oligarch,” wrote Ruffalo. “They are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.”
Paramount, for its part, responded by accusing Ruffalo of using “ antisemitic tropes ” in his argument, especially when linking the Ellisons’ studio acquisition to Oracle’s work with the Israeli military.

Ironic considering South Park Studios uses animation software with AI built into it, which was developed by billionaires and runs on machines and hardware manufactured and distributed by billionaires to be released onto another billionaire’s networks and streaming services funded by the billionaires who keep them in business by purchasing ad space.

articles.title_orig: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.title_zh: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.title_zh: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.
South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".
Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."
South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.
In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.
Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations".
As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015.
"Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says.
The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

Constitutional law attorney Jonathan Turley joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to break down the legal battle over New York City’s controversial pied-à-terre tax after a judge blocked its implementation.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday quickly appealed a judge’s decision to cancel previously mailed notices for his second-home tax, triggering an automatic stay of the ruling.
"The auto stay allows the city to continue, as we have been, with the implementation of the pied-a-terre surcharge and puts the lower court’s order on pause," a city official said.
Just hours earlier, Judge Wayne Ozzi found that the city failed to follow required procedures before mailing the notices, which he described as "arbitrary and capricious, affected by errors of law, and in violation of the recipients’ due process rights," according to the ruling.
Despite the ruling, Ozzi noted that the policy itself could still survive. He said the city can still apply the tax by removing the current list of taxed properties from its website and posting a corrected list after following the proper procedures.
MAMDANI’S LUXURY-HOME TAX ROLLOUT DERAILED FOR NOW AS JUDGE DELIVERS WIN TO NYC HOMEOWNERS OVER MASSIVE LIST
A spokesperson for Mamdani defended the tax as a "basic principle of fairness" for funding city services. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images/File)
New notices must then be mailed in compliance with the law.
Tuesday's decision served as a legal speed bump for Mamdani as he approaches nearly a year since he was elected New York City mayor and is among a handful of other legal challenges he faces as he attempts to implement government-first approaches to promises to bring down costs of living, expand housing and increase public transportation.
In addition to his second-home tax, Mamdani has also faced legal pushback on his rent freeze plan, which landlords have characterized as overly punitive, his state-sponsored grocery store plan, which has sparked challenges from the National Supermarket Association and what they see as unfair competition and challenges to specialized high school admissions that some parents believe unfairly discriminates against Asian-American enrollees.
Mamdani announced the second-home tax back in April.
In its original form, it was designed to levy an annual surcharge on one to three family homes, condominiums and co-ops valued at above $5 million. It also only applied to owners who also had additional property outside of New York City.
MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'

Alongside the governor, our administration is fighting every day to make sure we address this fiscal deficit fairly, where the wealthy contribute what they owe and our budget reflects our commitment to the working New Yorkers being priced out of our city," Mamdani said in a press release at the time.
Asked about the plan after Tuesday's decision, representatives for Mamdani said the mayor would stand by his plan.
Matt Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, defended the tax rollout, arguing that the pied-à-terre surcharge is a "basic principle of fairness" that supports a city he said should not be a "tax haven for the wealthy few."
"If you can afford a luxury second home in New York City, you can afford to pay your fair share for the schools, streets and parks that make this city work," Rauschenbach said.

articles.title_zh: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order , external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.
In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.
He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .
